introduction-speaking-the-cfos-language.core: Engineers think in performance and agility; CFOs think in CAPEX vs OPEX, depreciation and EBITDA. Cloud moves spending from capital to operating expense, which can hurt reported profitability even when it saves cash.

first_principles.problem: A CTO proposes a cloud migration expecting applause, but the CFO objects because EBITDA will drop.

analogy.title: Buying a car vs. leasing one
analogy.story: Buying shows up as an asset that slowly depreciates; leasing is a monthly expense that hits profit straight away.
analogy.breaks: This isn't accounting advice. Rules (GAAP, IFRS) and company policies vary.

example.title: The migration conversation
flow: Joint model: capitalise migration labour, show TCO
example.outcome: engineers can argue in financial terms.

check.q: Why might a CFO resist a cloud migration that saves money?
check.a: Moving from CAPEX to OPEX can lower EBITDA, a key metric investors watch.

capex-vs-opex-the-definitions.core: CAPEX buys long-lived assets (servers, buildings) recorded on the balance sheet and expensed gradually. OPEX is day-to-day running cost (cloud bills, salaries, rent) expensed immediately.

first_principles.problem: Engineers use the terms loosely and misjudge their financial impact.
truths: Assets provide value over many years.
Accounting matches expense to the period of benefit.
Cloud consumption is a service, not an asset.
derivation: **CAPEX**: upfront purchase → asset → depreciated over its useful life.
Consider the effect on **cash flow vs P&L**.

analogy.title: Buying a house vs. paying rent
analogy.story: The house is an asset you own and depreciate; rent is gone each month.
analogy.breaks: Some cloud commitments (prepaid RIs) can be treated as prepaid expenses, not CAPEX.

example.title: Buying servers vs. renting the cloud

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Cash out differs hugely from expense recognised.

check.q: Is a monthly AWS bill CAPEX or OPEX?

depreciation-vs-amortization-spreading-t.core: Depreciation spreads the cost of tangible assets (servers) over their useful life; amortisation does the same for intangible assets (capitalised software, licences). Cash leaves at once, but the expense is recognised gradually.

first_principles.problem: A $5M purchase seems to 'cost' $5M this year to engineers, while finance sees $1M a year.
truths: Matching principle: expense when the benefit is received.
Useful-life assumptions drive the annual expense.
derivation: **Depreciation**: tangible (servers, network gear), e.g. 5-year straight line.

analogy.title: Spreading a gym's equipment cost over its lifetime
analogy.story: A $50k treadmill bank that lasts 5 years 'costs' $10k a year in the books.
analogy.breaks: Extending useful life (e.g. servers from 4 to 6 years) changes reported profit without changing reality.

example.title: Servers vs capitalised software

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Big investments show up as modest annual expenses.

example.outcome: you understand how big purchases show up in profit.

check.q: What's the difference between depreciation and amortisation?
check.a: Depreciation applies to tangible assets; amortisation applies to intangible assets.

the-ebitda-trap.core: EBITDA excludes depreciation and amortisation, so on-prem hardware costs vanish from it, while cloud bills (OPEX) reduce it in full. Migrating to the cloud can make EBITDA worse even if the total cost is lower.

first_principles.problem: A company saves money overall by moving to the cloud, yet its valuation (an EBITDA multiple) drops.
truths: Investors value companies on EBITDA multiples.
CAPEX costs hide below EBITDA as D&A.
derivation: Valuation at **10x EBITDA** magnifies the effect.
Make the case with **cash flow and TCO** as well.

analogy.title: A scorecard that ignores some costs
analogy.story: If the scorecard leaves out equipment depreciation, renting equipment looks worse than owning it, even when renting is cheaper.
analogy.breaks: Sophisticated investors also look at free cash flow, and EBITDA isn't everything.

example.title: A migration's EBITDA effect

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Present cash and EBITDA effects together.

example.outcome: cloud proposals anticipate the EBITDA objection.

check.q: Why does moving to the cloud often reduce EBITDA?
check.a: Cloud costs are OPEX deducted before EBITDA, while on-prem hardware costs appear as depreciation, which EBITDA excludes.

financial-engineering-capitalizing-softw.core: Engineering salaries for building new long-lived software (features, platforms, migrations) can often be capitalised as an intangible asset and amortised, moving cost from OPEX to below EBITDA and offsetting the cloud's EBITDA hit.

first_principles.problem: All engineering time is expensed as OPEX, so heavy platform investment looks like pure cost.
truths: Accounting rules allow capitalising development of internal-use software.
Only certain phases qualify (development, not research or maintenance).
It requires time tracking and documentation.
derivation: **Capitalise** the eligible labour and amortise it over its useful life.

analogy.title: Building your own furniture
analogy.story: The labour that went into building a durable bookcase becomes part of the asset's value, not a one-off expense.
analogy.breaks: Maintenance, bug fixes and research usually can't be capitalised, and misuse invites audit trouble.

example.title: A migration programme

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The investment shows up as an asset, not a loss.

example.outcome: engineering investment is reflected accurately in financials.

check.q: Which engineering work typically can't be capitalised?
check.a: Maintenance, bug fixes and early research or feasibility work.

putting-it-together-the-finops-financial.core: A mature model combines everything: TCO (cash), the P&L view (OPEX vs D&A, EBITDA), capitalised labour, commitments as prepaid expenses and unit economics, so engineering and finance decide with the same numbers.

first_principles.problem: Engineering shows TCO, finance shows EBITDA, and they talk past each other.
truths: All the views derive from the same underlying costs.

analogy.title: A building project's full business case
analogy.story: Construction cost, financing, tax treatment and rent per square foot, all in one plan.
analogy.breaks: Models rest on assumptions, so show sensitivities.

example.title: A board-ready migration case
example.outcome: decisions grounded in a shared financial picture.

check.q: Why include both TCO and EBITDA views in a cloud business case?
check.a: TCO shows the real cash cost, while EBITDA shows the reported profitability investors judge, and both influence the decision.
